title: Imports and Namespace Setup
content: Imports the full Mathlib library and opens `BigOperators` (for `∑` notation), `Nat` scoped, `Filter`, and `Topology` namespaces. The formalization uses `Nat.nth` for prime enumeration, `Finset.range`/`Finset.Icc` for partial sums, `Tendsto` and `atTop` for limit statements, and `Real.log` for the Prime Number Theorem.
mathContext: Uses `Nat.nth Nat.Prime` for $p_n$, `Finset.range`/`Finset.Icc` for $\sum_{n=0}^{N}$ and $\sum_{n=a}^{b}$, `Tendsto f atTop (𝓝 L)` for $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(n) = L$.

title: The $n$-th Prime via `Nat.nth`
content: Defines $p_n$ as `Nat.nth Nat.Prime n`, the $n$-th element of the set $\{2, 3, 5, 7, 11, \ldots\}$ in increasing order (0-indexed: $p_0 = 2$, $p_1 = 3$, etc.). `Nat.nth` is Mathlib's general enumeration function for decidable predicates on $\mathbb{N}$, selecting the $n$-th element satisfying the predicate.
mathContext: $p_n = \text{Nat.nth}(\text{Nat.Prime}, n)$. The Prime Number Theorem gives $p_n \sim n \ln n$ as $n \to \infty$.

title: Alternating Prime Term $a_n = (-1)^n \cdot n/p_n$
content: The $n$-th term of the alternating series: $a_n = (-1)^n \cdot n / p_n$ for $n \ge 1$, with $a_0 = 0$. By PNT, $|a_n| = n/p_n \sim 1/\ln n \to 0$, so the terms vanish — a necessary condition for convergence. The alternating sign $(-1)^n$ creates cancellation between consecutive terms, but the non-monotonicity of $n/p_n$ prevents the Leibniz test from applying directly.
mathContext: $a_n = (-1)^n \cdot n/p_n$. For large $n$: $|a_n| \sim 1/\ln n \to 0$. The partial sums $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n$ appear to converge to $\approx -1$.

title: Partial Sums $S_N$
content: The $N$-th partial sum $S_N = \sum_{n=0}^{N} a_n$, computed via `Finset.range (N+1)` and BigOperators `∑` notation. The convergence question asks whether $\{S_N\}$ has a limit as $N \to \infty$.

title: Convergence Definition
content: The main conjecture: $\exists L \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $S_N \to L$ as $N \to \infty$, formalized via Mathlib's `Tendsto alternatingPrimePartialSum atTop (𝓝 L)`. This asks for convergence in the topological sense (every neighborhood of $L$ eventually contains all $S_N$).
mathContext: $\text{AlternatingPrimeSeriesConverges} \iff \exists L : S_N \to L$. The series does NOT converge absolutely ($\sum n/p_n \sim \sum 1/\ln n = \infty$), so if it converges, it does so only conditionally.

title: Prime Number Theorem: $p_n/(n \ln n) \to 1$
content: The foundational result of analytic number theory: $p_n \sim n \ln n$ as $n \to \infty$. First proved independently by Hadamard and de la Vallée-Poussin in 1896 using complex-analytic methods (non-vanishing of $\zeta(s)$ on $\Re(s) = 1$). Elementary proofs by Erdős and Selberg (1949). The PNT implies $n/p_n \sim 1/\ln n \to 0$, establishing the necessary condition for the alternating series.
mathContext: $p_n / (n \ln n) \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$. Equivalent to $\pi(x) \sim x/\ln x$ where $\pi(x)$ counts primes $\le x$.

title: Terms Tend to Zero: $n/p_n \to 0$
content: A direct consequence of PNT: $n/p_n \sim 1/\ln n \to 0$. This is the necessary condition for convergence of any series. The rate of decay $1/\ln n$ is very slow — much slower than $1/n$ — which is why the series does not converge absolutely.
mathContext: $n/p_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. The decay rate $1/\ln n$ means $\sum n/p_n \sim \sum 1/\ln n = \infty$ (divergent).

title: Alternating Terms Vanish: $|a_n| \to 0$
content: The absolute values $|a_n| = n/p_n \to 0$. This is necessary for convergence but not sufficient — the Leibniz test additionally requires monotone decrease of $|a_n|$, which fails here due to prime gap irregularity.
mathContext: $|(-1)^n \cdot n/p_n| = n/p_n \to 0$. Necessary condition for $\sum a_n$ to converge.

title: Non-Monotonicity of $n/p_n$
content: The sequence $n/p_n$ is NOT monotonically decreasing, which prevents the Alternating Series Test (Leibniz criterion) from applying. The failure occurs near twin primes: at $(p_5, p_6) = (11, 13)$, we have $5/11 \approx 0.4545 < 6/13 \approx 0.4615$, so the ratio increased. More generally, when $p_{n+1} - p_n = 2$ (twin prime gap), the numerator increases by 1 while the denominator increases by only 2, potentially causing an increase in the ratio.
mathContext: $\neg(\forall n \ge 1 : (n+1)/p_{n+1} \le n/p_n)$. Counterexample: $5/11 < 6/13$. The condition $(n+1)/p_{n+1} > n/p_n$ holds iff $p_{n+1}/p_n < (n+1)/n$, i.e., the prime gap is small relative to $p_n/n$.

title: Hardy–Littlewood Prime $k$-Tuples Conjecture
content: A deep unsolved conjecture predicting the density of prime constellations. For any **admissible** $k$-tuple $(h_1, \ldots, h_k)$ — meaning no single prime $p$ divides all residues modulo $p$ — there are infinitely many $n$ such that $n + h_1, \ldots, n + h_k$ are all prime. The formalization uses the admissibility condition: the image of $h$ modulo $p$ does not cover all residues $\{0, \ldots, p-1\}$ for any prime $p$.
mathContext: For admissible $(h_1, \ldots, h_k)$: $\#\{n \le x : n+h_1, \ldots, n+h_k \text{ all prime}\} \sim \mathfrak{S}(h_1, \ldots, h_k) \cdot x/(\ln x)^k$ where $\mathfrak{S}$ is the singular series.

title: Tao's Conditional Convergence (2023)
content: Terence Tao proved in 2023 that the alternating prime series converges, **assuming** the Hardy–Littlewood prime $k$-tuples conjecture. This is the best known result on Problem #15. Tao's approach uses the Hardy–Littlewood prediction to control the cancellation between consecutive terms: the conjecture provides enough regularity in prime distribution to bound the oscillation of partial sums. The result is conditional — removing the hypothesis is the open problem.
mathContext: $\text{HardyLittlewood} \Rightarrow \exists L : S_N \to L$. The proof uses the predicted asymptotic for twin prime density to bound $|S_{N+1} - S_N|$ and show the partial sums form a Cauchy sequence.

title: Prime Gap $g_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$
content: The gap between consecutive primes: $g_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$. By PNT, $g_n = o(p_n)$ on average, but $g_n$ can be as small as 2 (twin primes) or as large as $\sim \ln^2 p_n$ (Cramér's conjecture). The irregularity of $g_n$ is the fundamental obstacle to proving convergence of alternating prime series.
mathContext: $g_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$. Average: $g_n \sim \ln n$. Known: $\liminf g_n \le 246$ (Maynard 2015). Cramér conjecture: $\limsup g_n / (\ln p_n)^2 = 1$.

title: Erdős Gap Conjecture 1: $\sum (-1)^n/(n \cdot g_n)$ Converges
content: Erdős conjectured that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^n / (n \cdot g_n)$ converges. Since $g_n \ge 1$ and the average gap is $\sim \ln n$, the terms are $\sim 1/(n \ln n)$, which is summable. But the alternating signs and irregular gaps make this non-trivial. This conjecture remains **open**.
mathContext: $\sum (-1)^n/(n g_n)$ converges. Heuristically, $1/(n g_n) \sim 1/(n \ln n)$ and $\sum 1/(n \ln n)$ converges (integral test), but the alternating structure complicates matters.

title: Erdős Gap Conjecture 2: $\sum (-1)^n/g_n$ Diverges (PROVED)
content: Erdős conjectured that $\sum (-1)^n / g_n$ diverges. This was **proved** using Zhang's bounded gaps theorem (2014): since infinitely many gaps $g_n \le H$ for some $H$, the terms $|1/g_n| \ge 1/H$ infinitely often, and the alternating signs cannot produce enough cancellation.
mathContext: $\sum (-1)^n / g_n$ diverges. Key: $\liminf g_n \le H < \infty$ (Zhang/Maynard) implies $|(-1)^n/g_n| \ge 1/H$ infinitely often, preventing the partial sums from converging.

title: Zhang's Bounded Gaps Theorem (2014)
content: Yitang Zhang's revolutionary 2014 result: $\liminf_{n \to \infty} g_n < \infty$. Specifically, $g_n \le 70{,}000{,}000$ for infinitely many $n$. This was the first proof that prime gaps are bounded infinitely often. Maynard (2015) and the Polymath 8 project improved the bound to $g_n \le 246$, and conditionally (assuming Elliott–Halberstam) to $g_n \le 6$. The twin prime conjecture asserts $g_n = 2$ infinitely often.
mathContext: $\exists H : \{n : g_n \le H\}$ is infinite. Zhang: $H = 70{,}000{,}000$. Maynard/Polymath: $H = 246$. Twin prime conjecture: $H = 2$.

title: Erdős Gap Conjecture 2 Is True
content: Bounded gaps (Zhang 2014) imply $\sum (-1)^n / g_n$ diverges. Since $g_n \le H$ for infinitely many $n$, the subsequence of terms with $|1/g_n| \ge 1/H$ does not tend to zero fast enough. More precisely, the alternating partial sums oscillate by at least $1/H$ infinitely often, preventing convergence.
mathContext: Bounded gaps $\Rightarrow |(-1)^n/g_n| \ge 1/H$ for infinitely many $n$, so $\sum (-1)^n/g_n$ fails the Cauchy criterion.

title: Not Finitely Resolvable
content: No finite computation can determine convergence: for any $N$, there exist two real-valued sequences $f$ and $g$ that agree with $a_n$ for all $n \le N$, yet one converges and the other diverges. This means the answer depends entirely on the infinite tail behavior, which is controlled by the deep structure of prime distribution.
mathContext: $\forall N, \exists f, g : (\forall n \le N, f(n) = g(n) = a_n) \wedge (\sum f_n \text{ converges}) \wedge (\sum g_n \text{ diverges})$.

title: No Absolute Convergence: $\sum n/p_n = \infty$
content: The series $\sum n/p_n$ diverges, so the alternating series cannot converge absolutely. By PNT, $n/p_n \sim 1/\ln n$, and $\sum 1/\ln n$ diverges (by comparison with the integral $\int_2^\infty dx/\ln x = \text{Li}(x) \to \infty$). Thus if $\sum (-1)^n \cdot n/p_n$ converges at all, it does so only conditionally.
mathContext: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n/p_n = \infty$ since $n/p_n \sim 1/\ln n$ and $\sum 1/\ln n$ diverges. The logarithmic integral $\text{Li}(x) = \int_2^x dt/\ln t \to \infty$.
